title: MQTT Protocol Internals: Publish/Subscribe, QoS 0/1/2 Guarantees & Last Will and Testament
goal: Master the dominant cloud telemetry protocol: deconstruct MQTT 3.1.1/5.0 packet layouts, variable-length integer encoding, QoS 0/1/2 delivery guarantees, and Last Will and Testament (LWT) disconnect detection.
recap: In Block 7, we engineered wireless networks (BLE, Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN, Thread). Today we begin Block 8: Industrial IoT Protocols & Cloud Telemetry, starting with MQTT, the standard messaging protocol for cloud IoT ingestion.

parts.title: MQTT Publish/Subscribe Architecture & Topic Tree Wildcards
say: Unlike HTTP (which is request/response and point-to-point), MQTT is a Publish/Subscribe messaging protocol brokered by a central server (e.g., Mosquitto, EMQX, AWS IoT Core).

Publishers and Subscribers are completely decoupled in three dimensions: Space (they do not need to know each other's IP address), Time (they do not need to be online simultaneously if persistent sessions are used), and Synchronization (publishing is asynchronous).
Topic namespaces are hierarchical strings separated by forward slashes (e.g., 'factories/us-east/line1/press/temperature').

Clients subscribe using wildcards: Single-Level Wildcard ('+') matches exactly one hierarchy level ('factories/+/line1/press/temperature'); Multi-Level Wildcard ('#') matches any number of trailing levels and MUST be placed at the very end of the topic ('factories/us-east/#').
parts.example: A subscriber listening on 'sensors/+/temp' receives 'sensors/room1/temp' and 'sensors/room2/temp', but ignores 'sensors/room1/sub/temp'. Listening on 'sensors/#' receives everything under 'sensors/'.
parts.output:
--- DAY 36 PART 1: MQTT TOPIC MATCHING & WILDCARDS ---
[TOPIC-EVALUATOR] Testing MQTT Topic Filter Rules:
  Pattern: "factories/+/line1/temp" vs Topic: "factories/us-east/line1/temp" -> [MATCH]
  Pattern: "factories/+/line1/temp" vs Topic: "factories/us-east/sub/line1/temp" -> [REJECT]

parts.tryIt: Explain why subscribing to the root topic '#' on a massive enterprise broker is an operational antipattern.

check.question: What is the key difference between the MQTT single-level wildcard (+) and multi-level wildcard (#)?
options: The '+' wildcard matches exactly one topic hierarchy level, whereas '#' matches any number of subordinate topic levels up to the end of the topic string.
The '+' wildcard is for numbers, while '#' is for strings.
The '+' wildcard is only supported in MQTT 5.0.
The '#' wildcard can be placed at the beginning of a topic string.
check.why: In MQTT, '+' matches a single level between slashes (e.g. 'a/+/c' matches 'a/b/c' but not 'a/b/d/c'). '#' matches any arbitrary depth of trailing levels and must be the final character in the topic filter.

parts.title: Variable-Length Integer Encoding & Packet Header Anatomy
say: Every MQTT packet consists of three parts: 1) Fixed Header (present in all packets); 2) Variable Header (present in select packets like CONNECT, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE); 3) Payload (the actual message data).
The Fixed Header is just 2 bytes minimum. Byte 1 contains the Packet Type (bits 4-7: CONNECT=1, PUBLISH=3, PUBACK=4, PINGREQ=12, DISCONNECT=14) and Flags (bits 0-3: DUP, QoS level, RETAIN).
Byte 2 onwards contains the Remaining Length field, which uses a compact Variable-Length Integer Encoding scheme.
In Variable-Length Encoding, each byte uses the lower 7 bits (0-127) to encode the number, and bit 7 (0x80) as a Continuation Bit indicating whether another length byte follows.
A 1-byte length encodes up to 127 bytes. A 4-byte length can encode payloads up to 268,435,455 bytes (256 MB) while consuming only 1 byte for small packets!
parts.example: To encode length 64: binary 0x40 (MSB=0, 1 byte). To encode length 321: byte 1 = (321 % 128) | 0x80 = 0xC1; byte 2 = (321 / 128) = 0x02. Encoded as [0xC1, 0x02].
parts.output:
--- DAY 36 PART 2: MQTT VARIABLE LENGTH INTEGER ENCODING ---

  Value:      127 -> Encoded (1B): [0x7f] -> Decoded: 127 [PASS]
  Value:      128 -> Encoded (2B): [0x80, 0x1] -> Decoded: 128 [PASS]
  Value:      321 -> Encoded (2B): [0xc1, 0x2] -> Decoded: 321 [PASS]
  Value:    16384 -> Encoded (3B): [0x80, 0x80, 0x1] -> Decoded: 16384 [PASS]

codeNotes.note: encodeVariableLength implements the official MQTT 3.1.1 7-bit continuation encoding algorithm.
decodeVariableLength reconstructs the integer using incremental 128x multipliers until bit 7 is clear.
Demonstrates that values under 128 bytes require only a single byte of length overhead.

parts.tryIt: Calculate the maximum number that can be encoded in 4 variable-length bytes (hint: 128^4 - 1).

check.question: How does MQTT encode the remaining length field in packet fixed headers?
options: Using a 1-to-4 byte variable-length encoding where the lower 7 bits encode data and the MSB indicates continuation.
As a fixed 32-bit big-endian integer.
As an ASCII decimal string.
Using Base64 encoding.
check.why: The MQTT specification mandates a variable-length scheme using 7 bits per byte for the value and bit 7 as the continuation flag. This minimizes overhead for small sensor payloads (1 byte) while permitting packets up to 256MB.

parts.title: Quality of Service (QoS 0 vs 1 vs 2): Guarantees & Handshakes
say: MQTT provides three distinct Quality of Service (QoS) levels defining delivery guarantees between publisher, broker, and subscriber.

QoS 0 (At most once / 'Fire and Forget'): The publisher sends the PUBLISH packet and forgets it. No acknowledgment is sent; no packet ID is assigned. If the network drops the packet, it is permanently lost. Used for high-frequency telemetry where occasional drops don't matter.

QoS 1 (At least once / 'Acknowledged Delivery'): The PUBLISH packet contains a unique 16-bit Packet ID. The broker MUST reply with a PUBACK packet containing the matching ID. The publisher keeps the packet in a retransmit queue until PUBACK is received. If a network glitch occurs, the publisher resends the packet, which can cause duplicate delivery at the subscriber.

QoS 2 (Exactly once / 'Assured Delivery'): Uses a 4-step handshake: 1) PUBLISH -> 2) PUBREC (Publish Received) -> 3) PUBREL (Publish Release) -> 4) PUBCOMP (Publish Complete). It guarantees no loss and zero duplicates, but incurs 4 network round trips and heavy latency.
parts.example: Temperature updates every 500ms use QoS 0. Alarm notifications use QoS 1. Financial fund transfers or OTA firmware boot commands require QoS 2.
parts.output:
--- DAY 36 PART 3: QUALITY OF SERVICE (QOS) MECHANICS ---
[MQTT-QOS] Delivery Guarantee Matrix:
  QoS 0 (At most once   ):
    Guarantee:       Best effort delivery (May drop)
    Handshake RTTs:  0 Round-Trips (PUBLISH only)
    Duplicate Risk:  NO
    Packet ID Field: OMITTED
  QoS 1 (At least once  ):
    Guarantee:       Guaranteed delivery (May duplicate)
    Handshake RTTs:  1 Round-Trips (PUBLISH + PUBACK)
    Duplicate Risk:  YES (Application must be idempotent)
    Packet ID Field: MANDATORY
  QoS 2 (Exactly once   ):
    Guarantee:       Strict single delivery (Zero duplicates)
    Handshake RTTs:  2 Round-Trips (PUBLISH + PUBREC + PUBREL + PUBCOMP)
    Duplicate Risk:  NO
    Packet ID Field: MANDATORY

codeNotes.note: QoSSpec details the trade-offs between delivery certainty, network round-trips, and duplicate risk.
QoS 1 requires the application layer to be idempotent because dropped PUBACKs cause retransmissions.
QoS 2 eliminates duplicates via its 4-step handshake at the expense of high latency over cellular/satellite.

parts.tryIt: Describe what happens when a client sends a QoS 1 packet, the broker receives it and publishes to subscribers, but the PUBACK packet is lost in radio noise.

check.question: Why must an IoT application subscribing to MQTT QoS 1 telemetry treat incoming messages as idempotent?
options: Because if the network drops the broker's PUBACK response, the publisher retransmits the message with the DUP flag set, causing duplicate delivery.
Because QoS 1 packets are automatically encrypted twice.
Because the broker deletes all messages every 60 seconds.
Because QoS 1 messages only arrive on weekends.
check.why: QoS 1 guarantees delivery by retransmitting if an acknowledgment is not received. If the broker receives the publish successfully but the returning PUBACK is lost in network noise, the publisher re-sends the packet, resulting in duplicate delivery at the subscriber.

parts.title: Keep-Alive Heartbeats & Last Will and Testament (LWT)
say: TCP connections can die silently (the 'half-open' socket state) if a cable is cut or battery power fails without sending a TCP FIN packet.
MQTT resolves this with two integrated mechanisms: 1) Keep-Alive Heartbeats; 2) Last Will and Testament (LWT).

During CONNECT, the client specifies a Keep-Alive interval in seconds (e.g. 60s). If no application traffic is sent within this window, the client transmits a tiny 2-byte PINGREQ packet; the broker replies with a 2-byte PINGRESP.

The 1.5x Multiplier Invariant: In the MQTT specification, the broker will only declare a client disconnected if no packets (telemetry or PINGREQs) are received within 1.5 times the Keep-Alive duration (e.g., 60s * 1.5 = 90 seconds).

Last Will and Testament: In the CONNECT packet, the client registers a Will Topic, Will QoS, and Will Message (e.g., topic 'devices/dev01/status', message 'OFFLINE_UNEXPECTED'). If the broker detects an ungraceful disconnect (timeout or socket error), the BROKER automatically publishes the Last Will message to alert the fleet.
parts.example: A smart lock connects with LWT: 'devices/lock12/status' = 'OFFLINE'. If someone pulls the power cord, the broker publishes 'OFFLINE' to cloud dashboards after 1.5x Keep-Alive, without the dead lock sending a byte.
parts.output:
--- DAY 36 PART 4: KEEP-ALIVE & LAST WILL AND TESTAMENT ---
[SIMULATION] Normal operation: packet received at 30 seconds.

[SIMULATION] Sudden hardware cable cut at t=30! Client silent...
[BROKER-TIMEOUT] No packets received for 90s (1.5x Keep-Alive limit of 90s EXCEEDED)!
[BROKER-ACTION] Client declared UNGRACEFULLY DISCONNECTED.
  -> Publishing Last Will and Testament to Topic: "devices/smartlock_01/status"
  -> LWT Payload: "STATUS: UNEXPECTED_POWER_LOSS" (QoS 1)

codeNotes.note: LWTConfig registers the topic, message, and QoS registered during the initial CONNECT packet.
The broker enforces the 1.5x multiplier before disconnecting the client and triggering LWT.
Crucially, the Last Will message is transmitted by the BROKER on behalf of the dead client.

parts.tryIt: Explain why a graceful disconnect (sending DISCONNECT packet before closing socket) cancels the Last Will and Testament.

check.question: Who physically transmits the Last Will and Testament (LWT) message across the MQTT broker to alert subscribers when a client dies?
options: The MQTT broker transmits the LWT message automatically on behalf of the client when it detects an ungraceful disconnection or Keep-Alive timeout.
The dying client sends it right before its battery dies.
The Wi-Fi router generates the LWT message.
The user's smartphone sends the message.
check.why: A device that experiences a sudden power loss, battery drop, or broken cable cannot transmit a message. The broker stores the LWT parameters registered during CONNECT and publishes the message itself when it detects the client has dropped.

parts.title: Master Engine: Embedded MQTT Client in C++
say: We now construct the complete Day 36 Master Engine: an embedded MQTT Client platform.

Our engine models: 1) Construction of fixed and variable header byte sequences; 2) QoS 1 state machine tracking Packet IDs and processing incoming PUBACKs; 3) Keep-Alive timer management with PINGREQ transmission; 4) Last Will and Testament registration.
This architecture represents the core engine powering industrial telemetry gateways reporting to AWS IoT Core, Azure IoT Hub, and local Mosquitto servers.
parts.example: Executing the engine demonstrates CONNECT with LWT, QoS 1 publish with PUBACK handshake verification, and Keep-Alive heartbeat generation.
parts.output:

codeNotes.note: EmbeddedMQTTClient manages protocol states, packet ID generation, and Keep-Alive timing.
publishQoS1 assigns a 16-bit packet ID and validates matching PUBACK from the broker.
checkKeepAlive transmits 2-byte PINGREQ packets before the Keep-Alive window expires.

parts.tryIt: Add message retransmission logic: if PUBACK is not received within 2 seconds, resend with the DUP flag set.

check.question: What is the primary function of the MQTT PINGREQ and PINGRESP packets?
options: They allow the client and broker to verify that the underlying TCP connection remains open when no application data is being exchanged.
They calibrate the microcontroller real-time clock.
They query the current price of cloud storage.
They restart the microcontroller CPU.
check.why: PINGREQ (from client) and PINGRESP (from broker) are 2-byte heartbeat packets exchanged during idle periods to prove that the TCP link is alive and prevent the broker from triggering the client's Last Will and Testament.

summary: MQTT decouples publishers and subscribers across space, time, and synchronization via a central broker.
Topic filters support single-level (+) and multi-level (#) wildcards for dynamic hierarchical telemetry routing.
Fixed headers use a 7-bit variable-length integer encoding to support remaining lengths from 1 byte to 256 MB.
QoS 0 provides best-effort, QoS 1 guarantees delivery with duplicate risk, and QoS 2 guarantees exactly-once via a 4-step handshake.
Brokers enforce a 1.5x Keep-Alive timeout, publishing the client's Last Will and Testament if ungraceful disconnection occurs.

projectStep.title: Deploying an Embedded MQTT Client in C
steps: Initialize the network socket interface using non-blocking LwIP TCP sockets.
Construct an MQTT CONNECT packet registering client ID, Keep-Alive interval, and Last Will and Testament.
Implement QoS 1 telemetry publishing with 16-bit Packet ID tracking and a retransmission timeout buffer.
Schedule a periodic software timer to send 2-byte PINGREQ packets during idle intervals.
